entries.title: A dozen who will dazzle: A look at some top high school football stars on offense
entries.summary: <p>Two years ago, Nazareth’s Logan Malachuk broke the IHSA record for career passing yards. Last year, Lincoln-Way East’s Jonas Williams (who started his career at Bolingbrook) broke Malachuk’s mark.</p><p>While they’re both playing college ball, we’re still in a golden age for quarterbacks in the area.</p><p>Here’s a list, in alphabetical order, of 12 offensive players to watch in the 2026 season, including some elite quarterbacks.</p><h3><b>Israel Abrams, Montini</b></h3><p>The 6-4, 187-pound senior is the No. 2 player in Illinois, the No. 3 quarterback in the nation and the No. 32 player overall in the 247Sports composite rankings. A consensus five-star prospect committed to Miami, he led the Broncos to a 14-0 record and the Class 4A title last season. Abrams passed for 4,072 yards and 40 touchdowns with six interceptions and ran for 224 yards and 10 TDs.</p><h3><b>Grant Bowen, IC Catholic</b></h3><p>Miami, Michigan, Ohio State, Alabama, LSU and Ole Miss are just a few of the powerhouses that have offered scholarships to the 6-4, 220-pound junior. Last season, the two-way standout had 34 catches for 731 yards and 11 TDs, along with 55 tackles. Bowen is ranked 51st nationally and fourth in Illinois.</p><h3><b>Quinton Burrell, Mount Carmel</b></h3><p>Half of the best wide-receiver tandem in the state (with Marshaun Thornton), Burrell already is the four-time defending state champion Caravan’s career receiving leader in TD receptions. He has 34 TD catches to go along with 142 catches for 2,396 yards. The 6-3, 200-pound senior is a consensus top-100 player nationally and is committed to Michigan.</p><h3><b>Mason Halliman, Lincoln-Way East</b></h3><p>The 6-3, 275-pound lineman picked Illinois from more than 15 Power Four scholarship offers. He’s ranked 20th in Illinois in the 2027 recruiting cycle.</p><h3><b>Bennett Konkey, Geneva</b></h3><p>Maybe the fastest player in the state, Konkey is the reigning IHSA track champion in the 100 and 200 meters. The 6-1, 190-pound senior is committed to Illinois for football and has 70 catches for 1,298 yards and 15 TDs in the last two seasons.</p><h3><b>TJ Lewis, Bolingbrook</b></h3><p>The 6-foot, 225-pound running back is the reigning Southwest Prairie MVP. The Oklahoma State commit helped lead the Raiders back to prominence last season, piling up 1,808 all-purpose yards and 22 TDs.</p><h3><b>Jake Nawrot, Hersey</b></h3><p>The 6-4, 200-pounder is one of the most accurate passers in the state. He had a 71% completion rate with only two interceptions last season to go along with 3,078 yards and 41 TDs. The Kentucky commit is the consensus No. 3 senior in the state, the No. 5 quarterback nationally and the No. 65 player overall.</p><h3><b>Jameson Purcell, Maine South</b></h3><p>The 6-2, 200-pound lefty took over as the Hawks’ starter during his sophomore year. He has thrown for 5,443 yards and 58 TDs with 16 interceptions in the last two seasons. He’s committed to defending national champ Indiana.</p><h3><b>Marshaun Thornton, Mount Carmel</b></h3><p>A 6-2, 180-pound junior, Thornton is the other half of the Caravan’s game-breaking wide-receiver duo. He has more than 25 scholarship offers, including from Miami, Notre Dame, Indiana, Michigan, Illinois, Oregon and Ole Miss. The consensus No. 9 junior in the state had 48 catches for 881 yards and 16 TDs last season.</p><h3><b>Wyatt VanBoening, Carmel</b></h3><p>The 6-7, 290-pound junior tackle has an 84-inch wingspan. His scholarhip offers include Indiana, Notre Dame, Illinois and Iowa, among others. He is a top-80 player nationally in the 2028 cycle.</p><h3><b>Dominic Vita, Providence</b></h3><p>The 6-3, 205-pound junior was one of the top dual-threat quarterbacks in the area as a sophomore, completing 67% of his passes for 1,906 yards and 15 TDs and running 118 times for 520 yards and eight TDs.</p><h3><b>Brock Williams, Libertyville</b></h3><p>Williams was good enough to be a recruiting target for Texas. The 6-4, 215-pound Longhorns commit is the No. 5 senior in the state and the No. 90 player nationally. In the last two seasons, he has 79 catches for 1,204 yards and 18 TDs.<br></p>

entries.title: Ja Rule postgame concert canceled during ninth inning of White Sox game at Rate Field
entries.summary: <p>Boos rained down hard Friday at Rate Field as it was announced to fans watching the White Sox-Guardians game that the scheduled postgame concert featuring rapper Ja Rule had been canceled.</p><p>The bad news flashed on the center field scoreboard in the ninth inning, leading some fans to stream for the exits as the Sox trailed 8-2.</p><p>Again, booing — a lot of it.</p><p>"Unfortunately, the organization was just made aware that due to unexpected travel issues, Ja Rule is unable to make tonight's scheduled performance," the announcement read. "The concert has been canceled. Fans who have tickets to tonight's game will receive complimentary tickets to a future game. All field passes will be refunded. An email with more information will be sent to ticket holders in the next 72 hours."</p>
entries.author: Steve Greenberg

entries.title: The Sky's Sydney Taylor is made for this moment
entries.summary: <p>This was when it all hit home. All of it. The moment, the season, her career.</p><p>Thus far.</p><p>While Sydney Taylor dripped in the water her teammates had just doused on her once she entered the locker room after draining the three-pointer that gave the Sky a must-win victory against the defending champion Aces, coach Tyler Marsh stood in front of his team and let open.</p><p>‘‘We’ve been working our ass off all year, man. All year for a win like this. The fight and the faith that we got, like, Syd, I mean . . . ’’</p><p>There was no need to say any more. Minutes later, he tossed Taylor the game ball and bestowed the Flavor Flav plastic gold Sky logo-ed lei around her neck. Anointed.</p><p>There’s difference between an opportunity and a canvas. In this fairy-tale odyssey of Taylor’s basketball life, this most recent chapter should not be misunderstood as the WNBA or the Sky giving her an opportunity. It doesn’t work that way when it comes to her.</p><p>Opportunities are risks. She’s so far from removed from that.</p><p>This is about a team (and a league) being smart enough to realize when all a great artist needs is a large piece of canvas where she can go to work. Leave her alone. Let her be her. And soon after, the world will notice. Taylor has become both case and point.</p><p>Here she comes to save the day. Save the team. Save the season. Save the future. She came as a mystery. Ground zero. Becoming the feel-good story to erase those abdominal-wrenching losses, the organizational drama, the onslaught of injuries (of which she recently became a victim of with a minor groin injury), etc. The breath of fresh air the Sky organization and the Chicago basketball culture desperately needed.</p><p>Undrafted in 2024. Struggle, real. Got here and into the ‘‘W’’ on a signed training-camp contract in April. A contract that got her out of Turkey. Before there, she was hooping in Poland and Lithuania.</p><p>Maybe it’s the ‘‘no expectations’’ she stepped in the door with that has allowed her to flow and flourish with a sense of freedom the city hasn’t seen in a Sky uni since Kahleah Copper left. Maybe it’s the ‘‘no expectations’’ we put on her — which we’ve seemed to place the opposite on everyone else who has signed or been drafted to hoop here — that opened the door for her moment to arrive.</p><p>Her herstoric run since she slid Sky No. 12 on, so unexpected. Five games with 25 or more points so far. Giving herself her own ‘‘welcome to the W’’ moment. Evidenced by dropping 27 points in only 23 minutes in just her fifth career game in the league earlier this season. Two months later, she’s the WNBA’s player of the month. Ms. Hotter Than July.</p><p>‘‘She’s a hooper,’’ former WNBA game analyst and ‘‘Sportz Unplugged’’ podcast co-host Steve Bardo said, emphasizing the hooper part in every aspect and how surprised he is that a player of her ability went unnoticed and unselected before she arrived here. ‘‘When I first saw Sydney play, her movement efficiency jumped off the screen. She’s a special player.’’</p><p>Sarah Spain, she of the ‘‘Good Game With Sarah Spain’’ podcast and the content director of iHeart Women’s Sports, went further: ‘‘What [Sydney] represents is hope for a team and a fan base that needs it right now. So to have a surprise acquisition, someone who didn’t come with major expectations, that excites and wins and plays hard and does amazing things every night feels like a little bit of a gift.’’</p><p>There’s nothing ‘‘rookie’’ about her. Emerged as the Sky’s Option 1. Their PCA, CW’s 1 and 2, their Murakami. The Sky didn’t need a shero; better they got a show. Not ‘‘The Show’’ — that name was doled out to the ‘‘other’’ rook, Olivia Miles — but a show this city can’t afford to miss or ignore. One that we can only hope and pray doesn’t end anytime soon or doesn’t leave like so many of the other shows before her.</p><p>Sydney Taylor didn’t intentionally come here to be the Sky’s savior, but dammit if she’s didn’t take the cape. ‘‘Sydney Taylor’s Loud All-Rookie Push’’ of the WNBA’s ‘‘Five Things I Like: Week 10’’ article said as much: ‘‘The Sky have been desperately missing a shooter and driver of her caliber, and if they don’t emphasize her role in this offense, they’re looking at another lost season.’’</p><p>Lost but now no longer unfound.</p><p>‘‘Just because I wasn’t picked doesn’t mean I’m not chosen,’’ Ryan Clark’s T-shirt this week spoke. Read between those lines and know what Taylor has been and continues doing is far beyond just a player being undrafted.</p><p>Great artists, again, don’t accept opportunities; they create their own. And once a canvas is placed in front of them . . . masterpieces. Way too often in this game we call sports, the word ‘‘fate’’ is applied to . . . whatever. Overused and rarely applicable. But for Sydney Taylor’s moment in this country, in this city and for this team, fate couldn’t be more on-point than her crossing halfcourt with the ball leaving her fingers.</p><p>Or in a locker room being surrounded by teammates, holding down an organization, baptized in water with an oversized, fly faux gold cable link dripping from her neck.<br></p>

entries.title: 4 taken into custody after fight involving 2 off-duty Chicago police officers
entries.summary: <p>Four people were taken into custody after a fight broke out Friday afternoon near the 31st Street Beach involving two off-duty Chicago police officers, including one who suffered facial injuries, police said.</p><p>A 23-year-old man, a 24-year-old woman and two 22-year-old men were on a sidewalk at about 4:05 p.m. along the 3100 block of South Lake Shore Drive when two men and two women approached them, police said.</p><p>An argument took place between the groups, and the 23-year-old man and 24-year-old woman both identified themselves as officers and attempted to de-escalate the conflict, police said.</p><p>The dispute became physical, and the two men and two women who approached the group were taken into custody, police confirmed Friday night.</p><p>The male officer suffered cuts to his face and nose and was taken to a nearby hospital in good condition, police said.</p><p>One of the 22-year-old men suffered a cut to his forehead and the other suffered blunt-force trauma to his body. Both declined medical attention.</p><p>Charges were pending. Detectives are investigating.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: New Cubs pitcher gets ‘chills down my body’ from clutch Alex Bregman homer, also gets tips from home-run hero
entries.summary: <p>KANSAS CITY – Even if you couldn’t see <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/06/cubs-walk-off-win-alex-bregman-home-run-pete-crow-armstrong-stolen-base-blue-jays-dodgers-shohei-ohtani-nl-mvp" ><b>Alex Bregman</b>’s game-tying home run</a> Thursday, it was something special to be in the building for.</p><p>“That game, sitting there in the bullpen watching it,” righty reliever <b>Ryan Zeferjahn</b> said, “when Bregman hit that home run, I got chills down my body.”</p><p>Zeferjahn was closer than most of the more than 39,000 in attendance, but his view was more than a little blocked, obscured by the constraints of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/08/cubs-bullpen-ninth-inning-stats-jacob-webb-ryan-rolison-daniel-palencia-trent-thornton-tyler-ferguson" >Wrigley Field’s bullpen dungeon</a>.</p><p>“You can’t see. You can’t hear much,” Zeferjahn said. “You can hear a little bit. But you’ve got to go outside a few times between innings to get a feel.”</p><p>Despite the relievers being walled off from the rest of their teammates during games, there’s plenty of interaction with them at other times, even for the guys who just got here.</p><p>Zeferjahn, who was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-ryan-zeferjahn-bullpen-moises-ballesteros-trade-deadline-angels" >acquired in a trade-deadline deal</a> Monday, has already chatted with Thursday’s hero, Bregman living up to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/06/03/cubs-alex-bregman-free-agent-contract-astros-world-series-phil-maton-craig-counsell" >his reputation as a behind-the-scenes aid</a> for his teammates.</p><p>“Just seeing the professionalism, and the veteran group, the leadership, picking their brains,” Zeferjahn said. “Facing Bregman a couple times, … [he] was always one of the tough ABs for me. Seeing how he thought about me when I was throwing and working off that, how I can get better, is big for me. … Having that, being able to use that as a resource is very good.</p><p>“There’s going to be more [conversations]. … If there’s little things, I told him to come up and let me know and help me, because I’m always going to listen, I’m always going to learn, I’m always going to want to get better. That’s a big thing for me.”</p><p>Zeferjahn has gone head-to-head with Bregman three times, with Bregman getting a hit and drawing a walk and Zeferjahn logging a strikeout.</p><p>Zeferjahn has only been a Cub for a few days, but he’s already getting a crash course in how this team operates in a pennant race, from Bregman’s behind-the-scenes impact to the electric atmosphere at Wrigley Field. He pitched in two games during the Cubs’ <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/04/cubs-dodgers-three-peat-world-series-favorites-tarik-skubal-dansby-swanson" >three-game sweep of the Dodgers</a>.</p><p>He figures to be a key bullpen option for the Cubs down the stretch and into the postseason.</p><p>“That’s why we traded for him,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said. “We traded for him to pitch in those situations. You don’t control who you’re playing or the situation, but it’s what he’s here to do. So he’s in the game. He handled it all well, and I’m sure he had fun doing it.”</p><p><b>Shaw return ‘still weeks away’</b></p><p>Utility man <b>Matt Shaw</b> is only slowly progressing from the hand sprain that’s sidelined him since late June.</p><p>“We’re making progress, it’s just slow progress,” Counsell said. “It’s going in the right direction, just a lot more slowly than we would have hoped and [than we] thought. We’ve just got to be a little patient and not push it to a place where it does something negative.</p><p>“The [discomfort] of swinging a bat has lasted a lot longer than he thought and we thought. But we’re getting better. He’s swinging a little bit harder every day. We’ve just got to go slow.</p><p>“We’re still weeks away. He’s not swinging a bat at full speed. And we’ve missed enough games where there’s a significant rehab stint [necessary before he returns].”</p><p><b>Gausman gets hit</b></p><p>Righty starter <b>Kevin Gausman</b> made his Cubs debut Friday night and had a scary moment in his first inning with his new team, taking a line drive off his leg, near his ankle.</p><p>That sparked a visit from the trainer, but after several warm-up throws, Gausman stayed in the game.</p>

entries.title: White Sox manager Will Venable makes one of the gaffes of the season in loss to Guardians
entries.summary: <p>One thing seemed certain Friday as the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> opened a homestand against the American League Central rival Guardians at Rate Field, fresh — make that bone-weary — off a bonkers 12-11, 13-inning loss in Boston in the second-longest major-league game of the pitch-clock era (since 2023):</p><p>They needed starting pitcher Noah Schultz to hunker down and give them some innings.</p><p>Instead, Schultz got one out in a shaky first before his manager, Will Venable, committed one of the gaffes of the season by making a mound visit two batters after pitching coach Zach Bove went out there and, by rule, forcing Schultz’s removal from a game the Sox evenutally lost 8-2.</p><p>It was reminiscent of an epic gaffe by former Sox manager Terry Bevington in 1997 — also against Cleveland — when he trudged to the mound and motioned to the bullpen for a right-hander, despite the minor detail that nobody was warming up.</p><p>Venable seems pretty sharp on the whole, however, which made this a real surprise.</p><p>‘‘Just an inexcusable mistake by me where we had an appeal play that we wanted to execute and, in the urgency of trying to make that happen, just totally lost that we had visited,’’ he said. ‘‘Just messed it up.’’</p><p>Asked if someone on the bench had the task of rescuing him in such a scenario, Venable said: ‘‘It was just on me. That’s on me. Just a mistake by me and one of those you’ve got to learn from and can’t happen.’’</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Will Venable went out to talk with Noah Schultz, but the White Sox had already used one mound visit in the inning, so Schultz had to be removed from the game.<br><br>Schultz threw 23 pitches and only recorded 1 out. <a href="https://t.co/e7rnGMD3e4">pic.twitter.com/e7rnGMD3e4</a></p>— Just Baseball (@JustBB_Media) <a href="https://x.com/JustBB_Media/status/2085881046822682951?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 8, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>As the Sox took the field with four dozen games to go and a three-game lead over the Guardians and Twins in the AL Central, the last thing they needed was more negative momentum. Getting swept in three games by the Red Sox was plenty on that front — to say nothing of some of the developments therein, among them <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/05/white-sox-catcher-kyle-teel-davis-martin-tipping-pitches-red-sox" target="_blank" >Davis Martin seemingly tipping pitches</a> and rookie <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/06/chicago-white-sox-sam-antonacci-boston-red-sox-willson-contreras-chicken-wing-will-venable-alex-rodriguez-sonny-gray-bronson-arroyo" target="_blank" >Sam Antonacci chicken-winging Willson Contreras</a> on the basepaths.</p><p>Instead, they watched disaster unfold after David Sandlin — who was recalled from Triple-A Charlotte earlier in the day — had to get loose on the fly and take the mound for only the fifth time as a big-leaguer. Sandlin, the Sox’ No. 7-ranked prospect by <a class="Link" href="http://mlb.com/" target="_blank" ><u>MLB.com</u></a>, came through with a quality performance for a while before getting rocked by a grand slam by Angel Martinez in the Guardians’ five-run fifth. Sandlin left with the Sox trailing 8-1 in the sixth.</p><p></p><p>All of which has made it a tad harder to believe in the fortunes of a team that has played sub-.500 baseball since the All-Star break. Then again, welcome to the AL Central, where such stretches are a way of life. Only the Tigers were above .500 since the break, but they just waved the white towel by dealing mega-ace Tarik Skubal.</p><p></p><p>With four dozen games to go, a motto was suggested to some of the Sox: ‘‘48 Ours.’’</p><p></p><p>As in, let’s not screw up the rest of the season and we can raise a division banner.</p><p></p><p>‘‘Definitely,’’ Antonacci said. ‘‘There’s obviously still a lot of time left and a lot of things can happen, but we have the team to keep grinding and keep winning and put ourselves in a good spot. I think we’ve got a really good shot. It’s just: How bad do we want it?’’</p><p></p><p>Martin hasn’t been at his best since before the break, but he’s not backing down.</p><p></p><p>‘‘I like where my stuff is at,’’ he said. ‘‘It’s not a game for weak-minded people.’’</p><p></p><p>His eyes popped at the mention of ‘‘four dozen.’’</p><p></p><p>‘‘When you put it like that, it really doesn’t sound like [many left],’’ he said. ‘‘I think we’ve put ourselves in a great situation. We’ve weathered a lot of storms. We’re a good team.’’</p><p></p><p>Before the game, general manager Chris Getz noted much of this season came with a certain ‘‘baseball purity and innocence’’ for the Sox, who weren’t expected to amount to this much.</p><p></p><p>‘‘All of a sudden, you start paying attention to the standings or what another team is</p><p>doing, it’s a bit of a distraction,’’ Getz said.</p><p></p><p>The Sox might have been a distracted team in Boston. Their manager and his staff might not have been all that locked in Friday. That’s not going to get it done the rest of the way.</p><p></p><p>According to Venable, he was considering going to Sandlin after another couple of hitters anyway.</p><p></p><p>Schultz, however, said: ‘‘I was under the impression it would be a normal start.’’</p><p></p><p>There was nothing normal about this one.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/07/white-sox-joey-bart-chris-murphy-edgar-quero-david-sandlin-mlb" target="_blank" >White Sox send C Joey Bart, LHP Chris Murphy to injured list; recall C Edgar Quero, RHP David Sandlin</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: How does Edward Cabrera, on road back from hamstring injury, fit into Cubs’ pitching puzzle upon return?
entries.summary: <p>KANSAS CITY – The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> trading a top prospect for an impact starting pitcher is nothing new.</p><p>Jed Hoyer’s front office <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-top-prospects-trades-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-ryan-zeferjahn-braxton-garrett-tyrone-taylor" >got aggressive at the trade deadline</a> and shipped away a significant chunk of its top-30 prospect list – including No. 2 ranked Jefferson Rojas – for pitching, making a win-now statement in the process.</p><p>But rewind to the offseason, and Hoyer did the same thing, dealing outfield prospect Owen Caissie to the Marlins for righty starter Edward Cabrera, believing he could be a top-of-the-rotation arm for a championship-caliber group.</p><p>That was a win-now statement then, somewhat colored in hindsight by the fact that Cabrera hasn’t been that type of pitcher, not yet anyway. Injuries have had plenty to do with it, and after blister issues forced an IL stint, Cabrera has been out for more than a month rehabbing from a hamstring strain.</p><p>That rehab process is nearing its conclusion in the wake of the deadline and the addition of multiple pitchers to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/30/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-pitching-starting-rotation-matthew-boyd-shota-imanaga-colin-rea-david-peterson-javier-assad-tarik-skubal" >a Cubs rotation that’s currently thriving</a> – and seeming <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/04/cubs-pitching-starting-rotation-mlb-trade-deadline-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-jed-hoyer-craig-counsell-colin-rea-edward-cabrera-braxton-garrett" >overflowing with options for Craig Counsell</a> as the team steams toward the postseason.</p><p>With newly added righties Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes in the mix alongside lefties Matthew Boyd and Shota Imanaga – and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/28/cubs-david-peterson-mlb-trade-deadline-mets-jed-hoyer-pitching-staff-rotation-craig-counsell-ground-ball-rate" >lefty David Peterson pitching well, too</a> – does that leave room for Cabrera upon his return?</p><p>“Those are things that we don’t control,” Cabrera said of the team’s trade-deadline activity, through an interpreter Friday. “Those are things that people upstairs control, and if they believe that those were the additions that we needed, those are the decisions that they made.</p><p>“I know all of the guys, and I know they’re all really good players. I know they’re going to help us and contribute.”</p><p>The Cubs know you can’t have too much pitching, of course, and with righties Javier Assad and Colin Rea already shifted from needed fill-ins to depth pieces, they’re well prepared for the possibility – in this sport, maybe it’s an inevitability – that they’ll need to lean on that depth before season’s end.</p><p>But what becomes of Cabrera?</p><p>“I’m here to follow orders,” he said. “Whatever the boss says, whatever they need me to do, I’m going to follow the orders and do anything for the team. Whatever’s necessary.”</p><p>He’s working back with plans of being part of that starting group, and he had a strong first minor league rehab start Wednesday, throwing four scoreless innings.</p><p>But with visions of playoff baseball dancing in everyone’s heads, maybe Cabrera is a tantalizing relief possibility, as well?</p><p>“I think we’re definitely open to doing that,” pitching coach Tommy Hottovy said Thursday. “He’s got an electric arm. It’d be crazy not to think about him being able to come in in a postseason game and throw the back-end two to three innings of the game.</p><p>“It’s important for him to start right now, for sure, and continue to build up. … For us, our goal is to get him back as a starter.</p><p>“How things end up at the end of the year? You know how the postseason becomes, it’s an all-hands-on-deck approach, anyway.”</p><p>Since Hoyer’s work to stock the Cubs’ pitching cabinet, Counsell has said that any pitcher could be used out of the bullpen come the playoffs. All hands on deck, and all that.</p><p>There’s a lot of time to figure out who might be an odd man out of the starting staff come October. Until then, a six-man rotation could be a possibility, at times, but not on a regular basis.</p><p>Cabrera needs to wrap his recovery first, and another minor league rehab start is coming Tuesday with Double-A Knoxville. Once that work is complete, we’ll get a better idea of what the team plans for him and all their pitchers.</p><p>“The mindset is everybody here is ready to come together and work as one and go out there and give it our absolute best,” Cabrera said. “That’s the mindset that we’re buying into, which will be able to help us in the playoffs.</p><p>“I trust all of the guys here. We’re here as one, and we’re here to help the team out.”</p>

entries.summary: <h2>Moon alert</h2><p>There are no restrictions to shopping or important decisions today. entries.title: Trade-deadline addition Kevin Gausman shines in Cubs debut: ‘He’s nasty, he really is’
entries.summary: <p>KANSAS CITY – Jed Hoyer saw his trade-deadline work flash before his eyes Friday night.</p><p>The team president <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-top-prospects-trades-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-ryan-zeferjahn-braxton-garrett-tyrone-taylor" >got aggressive at the deadline</a> to bring in a couple top-of-the-rotation pitchers. Then the headline acquisition, righty starter Kevin Gausman, took a line drive off his ankle, in his very first inning in a Cubs uniform.</p><p>Thankfully for Gausman and the Cubs, the veteran righty was OK, staying in the game after a visit from the trainer and some warm-up throws.</p><p>“I got lucky,” Gausman said, “it hit me half on my shoe, half on my leg. I’ll take that.</p><p>“I’ll put some tape on it, put some ice on it the next couple days. I’ll be all right.”</p><p>Gausman was more than all right in his Cubs debut.</p><p>After a shaky first inning in which he walked the leadoff man, allowed two hits and gave up a run, he was almost perfect, surrendering just a solo homer and one other hit, retiring 19 of the final 21 batters he faced in seven strong innings and helping his new team to its fifth straight win, a 6-4 victory over the Royals.</p><p>“It seemed like he got stronger as he went,” catcher Carson Kelly said. “All in all, just a really, really good start. He’s nasty, he really is.</p><p>“He’s a huge piece. The intensity that he brings, the experience that he has, how to navigate a lineup, how to continue to take it to them, that’s something that’s very valuable for us.”</p><p>Prior to arriving in a trade with the Blue Jays, Gausman’s numbers weren’t as strong as they had been, though the Cubs weren’t concerned about his ERA jumping from 3.59 last season to 4.38 this year.</p><p>Gausman showed Friday that he’s still the guy who delivered in the postseason last fall.</p><p>While an early-August game against the last-place Royals is hardly the World Series, he looked like that kind of pitcher, a great sign for a Cubs team with championship-level aspirations.</p><p>“I noticed it right away coming over here, the excitement of the team, of the guys, of each other,” Gausman said. “It was nice to finally get out there and feel like I was part of the team.”</p><p>“We’re here to win baseball games,” Kelly said. “He’s a winning pitcher, a winning player. That’s something that’s going to help us along the way.”</p>

entries.title: Claire's revamps piercing experience for Gen Alpha, but brand nostalgia spans generations
entries.summary: <p>Teen accessories and jewelry retailer Claire’s said its stores will undergo a “glow-up,” one year after it filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. </p><p>The company, which moved from Hoffman Estates to Rosemont earlier this summer, plans to invest in its piercing services and in-store experience, starting this month. The transformation will happen across Claire’s 900 locations in the U.S. and Canada, according to a news release. The Chicago area has 19 locations, including one at Water Tower Place. </p><p>“We really do see [piercing] as a responsibility, not just a service," Claire's Vice President of Retail Operations Carey Brezler said. “It is a milestone moment, and it's a rite of passage for so many. ... entries.title: Nasty weather is understandable — but not United Airlines' nasty response
entries.summary: <p>On July 27, I flew from Charlotte, North Carolina, to Chicago to catch a connecting flight to Lincoln, Nebraska. My flight to Lincoln was scheduled to depart about 1 p.m.</p><p>After arriving at my assigned gate, I learned the flight was delayed due to weather conditions and was moved to another gate. When I arrived at the next gate, the flight was reassigned again. At the third gate, the same thing happened. At the final gate, passengers were informed the flight had been canceled.</p><p>I understand that weather can disrupt air travel, and airlines cannot control the weather. What concerns me is how passengers were treated afterward.</p><p>With thousands of travelers stranded, hotel rooms quickly became difficult to find. I booked a hotel online, took an Uber there and upon arrival, learned the hotel had double-booked the room. I then reserved a second hotel, took another Uber and found they had no record of my reservation. Left with no other options, I returned to O'Hare Airport.</p><p>The terminal was filled with stranded travelers. Families with small children, elderly passengers and exhausted travelers were sleeping on floors, benches and any available space because no additional flights were departing that night.</p><p>When I approached a United Airlines counter seeking assistance, a male employee loudly exclaimed, "We’re closed!" and walked away. Realizing I had no choice but to spend the night in the airport, I remained near the counter so I could speak with staff when they arrived the next morning.</p><p>About 4:15 a.m. when United employees started showing up, a female employee immediately shouted at me, “You need to get back behind the line!” When I tried to explain that I was simply seeking information after a sleepless night, she responded, “Everyone here is.” I later requested to speak with a supervisor and was told one would come. A supervisor never appeared.</p><p>After returning home, I filed a formal complaint with United. I was assured someone would contact me. No call came. Instead, I received a text message apologizing for the experience, along with an offer for a $75 travel voucher.</p><p>I'm not frustrated with the weather that led to the flight cancellation. I'm exasperated with the lack of communication, assistance, professionalism and respect shown to passengers when things took a wrong turn. Travelers deserve better.</p><p><i>Bil Roby-Tubach, Lincoln, Nebraska</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c00000" name="module-c00000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Emergency departments need better grip on children’s mental health </h3><p>Our emergency rooms are telling us something alarming about children's mental health. We should listen. A new <a class="Link" href="https://www.luriechildrens.org/en/news-stories/emergency-departments-across-illinois-identify-gaps-in-care-for-children-in-mental-health-crises/" target="_blank" >statewide survey of Illinois emergency departments</a>, led by Dr. Jennifer Hoffman of Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children's Hospital, offers one of the clearest pictures yet of what happens (and what doesn't happen) when a child arrives at an emergency department with a purported behavioral health crisis.</p><p>Emergency care coordinators across the state do their work with dedication and skill. But many survey respondents admittedly practice at hospitals with no dedicated pediatric inpatient unit, and only about half of those have a mental health professional on site. As summarized in the report, only 56% of such providers consistently deliver every recommended element of safety planning before a child goes home. Only 25% routinely schedule a follow-up mental health appointment before discharge. Even the most skilled emergency personnel are limited by their available resources.</p><p>Answers aren’t beyond reach or reason. The study highlights how many care teams have little-to-no sensible referrals or placements available, and that emergency staff are ill-equipped to meet certain needs that extend well beyond an immediate crisis. The result is prolonged boarding. Children wait in emergency departments, sometimes longer than three days, because there is nowhere else for them to go. We would not tolerate this for a child with an urgent physical injury. Why do we expect children with mental health conditions to simply endure?</p><p>An emergency room should be one door among many, not the only door. That means investing in the continuum around the hospital: mobile crisis teams, which research links to fewer repeat emergency department visits among youth; real-time visibility into psychiatric bed availability for quicker placements when appropriate; peer and family support that begins before a crisis and continues after discharge; and community settings where a young person can stabilize with dignity. It also means better support inside the ER while children wait and wait.</p><p>This is fixable. Coordination matters. So does dedicating real resources to it. Families, policymakers, health plans, hospitals, schools and community organizations all share responsibility for building a system where fewer children reach the ER in crisis. Above all, the study underscores that we can all do better for our children's mental health.</p><p><i>Matt Davison, CEO,</i> <i>NAMI Chicago</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-540000" name="module-540000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Listen to and embrace Black youth</b></h3><p>It’s time for an honest conversation about how we view young people in Chicago — particularly Black teenagers and young adults.</p><p>When Black youth are involved in “smash-and-grab” burglaries, shootings or so-called <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/06/04/teen-takeovers-black-south-west-sides-chicago-public-schools-robert-jordan" >“teen takeovers”</a> that turn violent, it’s front-page news. The result is a false and damaging perception that most of our young people are dangerous predators.</p><p>That’s why, even in one of America’s most progressive cities, some City Council members continue pushing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/04/29/revised-curfew-ordinance-brian-hopkins-brandon-johnson-teen-takeovers-downtown" >earlier curfews</a>, harsher penalties, incarceration and steep fines for young people <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/06/16/ald-ray-lopez-parental-responsibility-ordinance-city-council" >and their parents</a>. But how does jailing a struggling parent help a child? How do crushing fines on families already working 50 or 60 hours a week make neighborhoods safer?</p><p>Fortunately, Mayor Brandon Johnson has consistently pushed back against proposals rooted more in fear than in solutions.</p><p>The unfortunate reality is that many of the loudest voices demanding punishment over opportunity have little meaningful relationship with Black youth.</p><p>We do.</p><p>For decades, we have mentored, developed and invested in young people. At last month's meeting of <a class="Link" href="https://leadersnetworkchicago.org/" target="_blank" >the Leaders Network</a>, we turned the entire program over to our youth. They planned, hosted, prayed, performed and led thoughtful discussions. The adults did something we don’t do often enough — we listened.</p><p>What did we learn?</p><p>Our young people want what every generation has wanted: opportunities, meaningful relationships, new experiences and to be recognized for their potential rather than judged by the mistakes of a few.</p><p>No chairs were thrown. No windows were broken. No one was shot. No one was injured. Yet barely any media organizations covered the event.</p><p>That must change. Our young people deserve to see that being thoughtful, compassionate, articulate and solution-oriented is also newsworthy. They deserve stories that inspire hope instead of those that reinforce stereotypes.</p><p>Let us be clear: Violence must never be tolerated. We have spent years demanding accountability and offering reward money to help bring murderers to justice.</p><p>But law enforcement alone cannot bring lasting peace.</p><p>Peace requires opportunity, mentorship, investment and adults willing to believe in young people before demanding they believe in themselves.</p><p>The overwhelming majority of Chicago’s Black youth are students, workers, dreamers, athletes, artists, entrepreneurs, caregivers and future leaders.</p><p>We challenge the media to broaden its lens.</p><p>We challenge elected officials to prioritize opportunity alongside accountability.</p><p>And we challenge all of Chicago to show our young people what they desperately need — and richly deserve: Love</p><p><i>The</i> <i>Rev. Ira Acree, lead pastor, Greater St. John Bible Church, Austin</i></p><p><i>David Cherry, president, The Leaders Network </i></p><h3>Chicago can’t handle public-owned grocery store </h3><p>Undoubtedly, “food deserts” in Chicago must be addressed, but the city should not rush to open publicly owned grocery stores as a recent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/08/05/public-owned-grocery-store-sav-a-lot-food-desert-south-west-sides-erion-malasi" >op-ed</a> by Erion Malasi suggested.</p><p>The Sun-Times has extensively reported on the city of Chicago's mismanagement of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2025/01/07/cta-crime-fiscal-crisis-ridership-2025-dorval-carter-micky-horstman" >Chicago Transit Authority</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/07/23/chicago-public-schools-budget-deficit" >Chicago Public Schools</a> and the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/10/10/chicago-housing-authority-debra-parker-cha-contracts-investigation" >Chicago Housing Authority.</a></p><p>The city already struggles with transporting its citizens, educating its citizens and housing its citizens. Before setting out on any plan to feed its citizens, it should exhaust all other options before opening publicly owned grocery stores. .</p><p><i>Terry Takash, Western Springs</i></p><h3>Thieves don’t care who owns the grocery store</h3><p>City-owned grocery stores seem like a good idea. However, it may be wise to find out exactly why grocery stores in low-income neighborhoods are so apt to close down. Is it because low-income citizens buy fewer groceries? Are the stores poorly managed? What are the forces at work that make it unprofitable for stores to sell basic necessities that all humans must have?</p><p>How much does theft, from both customers and employees, contribute to stores losing money? If that is the biggest problem, it needs to be addressed, and in a definitive way. When I was a child we shopped at neighborhood grocery stores. We did not have access to the food directly, but gave a list to the proprietor or another employee and they got the food for us. We went to separate stores for meat and produce, which was given to us the same way. It would have been impossible to steal anything before supermarkets took over. Then shopping became much more efficient and enjoyable —and shoplifting became much more easy.</p><p>Even with supposedly more strict policing these days, a friend who works at a Downtown clothing store told me that people come in, stuff clothes into bags and quickly run out almost every day. The employees are told not to stop them, my friend says. The shoplifters have grown to feel entitled, and prices rise to cover the loss.</p><p>So, unless the elephant in the room is addressed, public-owned grocery stores will be a losing proposition for taxpayers.</p><p><i>Sharon Novickas, South Loop</i></p><h3>Sox fans in their pope hats will be memorable</h3><p>I can't wait for Tuesday when the White Sox take the field in front of a crowd of energized fans, thousands of them wearing, of all things, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/08/white-sox-pope-leo-pope-themed-hats-reds" >Pope Leo XIV-themed hats</a>. What will that look like? I can't even imagine, but I think the pope, the team's most famous fan, will be grinning from ear to ear. I'd love to get a photo of him taking it all in, his handsome and friendly face reflecting the joy and humor of a very creative day at the South Side baseball park.</p><p>Some may worry that this kind of demonstration might be offensive to Catholics or to the pope himself. I call it a wonderful, creative and joyful tribute to a very special White Sox fan who just happens to be leader of a major religion. I highly doubt that Pope Leo XIV would ever be offended by this humorous, yet respectful, tribute. The only thing that could outdo this display of pope hats is if Pope Leo XIV were sitting in the stands munching a hot dog smothered in mustard.</p><p><i>Kathleen Melia, Niles</i></p><h3>Appallingly Hitleresque </h3><h3></h3><p>Since Donald Trump loves to get awards, I would like to nominate him for one. I think he should get this year’s "Adolf Hitler Award." The criteria is looking for a "leader" whose actions most embody those used by Hitler.</p><p>It's an easy decision, given Trump's attacks and suppression of the press; his creation of an armed squad that terrorizes and kills immigrants and U.S. citizens; his demonizing a group of people and using them as the excuse for the country’s problems; his use of the military to start unjust wars and try to take over countries that don’t want to be a part of the United States; his use of his position to increase his own wealth; his placing of his picture everywhere; his demand of blind loyalty from his minions who can’t think for themselves and whose only qualification is that they kiss his ring; his disdain for the rule of law; his spreading of hate with every time he opens his mouth; and lastly but not least, his inability to accept responsibility for his actions.</p><p>For all these reasons, and more, he truly is the living example of Hitler and modern fascism.</p><p><i>Peter Felitti, Lincoln Square</i><br></p>

entries.title: Can would-be buyer afford to take over more Chicago-area hospitals?
entries.summary: <p>Insight Health Systems is interested in rescuing two closed Chicago-area hospitals, even as its hospital in Chicago appears to be struggling.</p><p>Since <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/environment-public-health/2021/10/25/inside-the-fight-to-save-chicagos-historic-mercy-hospital" target="_blank" ><u>buying historic Mercy Hospital</u></a> in 2021 for $1 — keeping it from closing — and changing its name to Insight Hospital and Medical Center, the hospital has consistently lost money, according to its tax returns. Located in Bronzeville, Insight had a nearly $30 million loss in 2024, its most recent records show.</p><p>And Insight Hospital has received about $50 million in advances from the Illinois Department of Healthcare and Family Services to help keep the doors open since it bought Mercy.</p><p>As recently as 2024, Insight Hospital faced a “financial emergency,” according to its advanced payment plan agreement WBEZ and the Chicago Sun-Times obtained through a public records request. The hospital ran into trouble with a contractor trying to upgrade its outdated billing system, causing “high levels” of unpaid bills from patients and health insurers. Add high labor costs and materials, and Insight faced potentially “significant cash flow problems,” the state found.</p><p>These records raise questions about how Insight Health Systems can afford to reopen and operate two more hospitals — West Suburban Medical Center in Oak Park and Weiss Memorial Hospital in Uptown. Their owner <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/03/25/west-suburban-medical-center-closing-runs-out-cash-weiss-memorial" target="_blank" ><u>suddenly closed</u></a> West Suburban in March and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2025/08/08/weiss-memorial-hospital-emergency-room-in-uptown-closes" target="_blank" ><u>Weiss in August 2025</u></a>, forcing patients to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2026/07/11/where-do-they-go-what-west-side-patients-face-after-another-hospital-closes-west-suburban-medical-center" target="_blank" ><u>travel farther for care</u></a> to hospitals already stretched thin.</p><p>Insight Hospital, West Suburban and Weiss are all safety-net hospitals, which are often the fabric of low-income and immigrant communities. They typically don’t make much money and struggle to make ends meet.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Black plastic went over the emergency room signs at West Suburban Medical Center in Oak Park after the facility closed in late March.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>An Insight Health Systems spokesperson declined an interview request, responding with a written statement that said the health system “has consistently demonstrated the commitment and willingness to step in where it can help close gaps in access.”</p><p>Insight Hospital is an independent nonprofit and would not be managing West Suburban, the statement said. Its parent company would. “Questions premised on Insight’s financial role in West Suburban’s reopening are therefore misplaced,” the statement said.</p><p>But the top executive at Insight Hospital — CEO Atif Bawahab — is chief strategy officer of <a class="Link" href="https://www.iinn.com/leadership/" target="_blank" ><u>Insight Health Systems</u></a>, a for-profit with several facilities in Michigan, according to their websites. Insight Hospital’s board chairman and two other <a class="Link" href="https://insightchicago.com/leadership/" target="_blank" ><u>board members</u></a> are also executives with the parent company, including Insight Health Systems’ chief financial officer.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/08/04/ownership-change-west-suburban-weiss-potential-settlement" target="_blank" ><u>Insight Health Systems’ interest</u></a> in taking over West Suburban and Weiss emerged in a messy divorce between the closed hospitals’ owners. The proposed settlement agreement says Insight essentially would buy the hospitals for $1 and manage them. State regulators would need to approve any ownership changes.</p><p>Insight Hospital has a small footprint in Chicago. The hospital treats mostly elderly and low-income patients. The majority are Black, public health data shows. In 2024, Insight had more than 1,000 employees to staff a hospital that, at its busiest time that year, <a class="Link" href="https://hfsrb.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/hfsrb/documents/inventories-data/hospital/facility-profiles/2024/2024-Hospital-Profiles-Individual.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>treated about 80 patients</u></a>, records show. That’s even though the hospital is licensed by the state to treat about five times more people, records show.</p><p>Shannon Bennett, executive director of the Kenwood Oakland Community Organization, known as KOCO, is among several community leaders, patients and former employees <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/07/28/weiss-west-suburban-hospital-pritzker-prasad" target="_blank" ><u>calling for</u></a> West Suburban and Weiss to reopen with a responsible leader — and for Gov. JB Pritzker and state lawmakers to help.</p><p>KOCO was a <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/environment-public-health/2021/03/05/community-organizers-push-for-say-in-mercy-hospitals-future" target="_blank" ><u>fixture at rallies</u></a> to save Mercy Hospital from closing. Now, Bennett sees how Insight is a resource in the community. He’s used the emergency room twice.</p><p>Told of Insight Hospital’s financial struggles, Bennett suggested the state support Insight to save two more hospitals and to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2026/07/27/a-new-illinois-law-keeps-hospital-finances-hidden-from-the-public" target="_blank" ><u>be transparent</u></a> about the process.</p><p>“We always get told why it can’t work or why something won’t work,” Bennett said. “Let's lead with the possibility of a Black community, a very integrated community in Uptown, having the opportunity to think through this with the people who normally don’t engage them.”</p><p>He sees Insight as a willing partner while also calling for vetting them to take on more.</p><p>He suggested the state offer debt relief for whoever operates West Suburban and Weiss. Their owner closed the hospitals owing the state <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2026/07/11/where-do-they-go-what-west-side-patients-face-after-another-hospital-closes-west-suburban-medical-center" target="_blank" ><u>more than $100 million.</u></a></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-dc0000" name="image-dc0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2f30cef/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6c%2F05%2Ff63e823b45b786df38ce75ab2f80%2Fwestsubfolo-260402-29.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/42eb5f3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6c%2F05%2Ff63e823b45b786df38ce75ab2f80%2Fwestsubfolo-260402-29.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7aff565/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6c%2F05%2Ff63e823b45b786df38ce75ab2f80%2Fwestsubfolo-260402-29.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="State Rep. La Shawn K. Ford (right) speaks about the future of the hospital alongside Resilience Healthcare CEO Manoj Prasad during press conference to answer questions about the hospitals closure on April 1, 2026." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7aff565/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6c%2F05%2Ff63e823b45b786df38ce75ab2f80%2Fwestsubfolo-260402-29.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/02fcf4e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6c%2F05%2Ff63e823b45b786df38ce75ab2f80%2Fwestsubfolo-260402-29.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7aff565/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F6c%2F05%2Ff63e823b45b786df38ce75ab2f80%2Fwestsubfolo-260402-29.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>State Rep. La Shawn K. Ford, on the right, on April 1 spoke about the hospital’s closing at a news conference with Resilience Healthcare CEO Manoj Prasad, the majority owner of West Suburban Medical Center.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>A spokeswoman for Pritzker declined an interview. State Rep. La Shawn Ford, D-Chicago, said he hasn’t heard of the state giving Insight money to take over West Suburban and Weiss. Other safety-net hospitals want state help, too, Ford said.</p><p>“Do we allow for them to fail?” he said of Insight possibly taking on two more struggling hospitals. “Or do we protect what’s open?”</p><p>To reopen the two hospitals, Insight would need to woo the community as well as nurses and doctors who might already have found new jobs. Leaders will need to figure out how to survive.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://cookcountyhealth.org/press-release/get-medicaid-facts-new-site-and-toolkit-launched-to-educate-public-about-looming-medicaid-eligibility-changes/" target="_blank" >Big cuts to Medicaid</a> public health insurance for people who are poor or have disabilities are coming next year. More than 400,000 people <a class="Link" href="https://www.rwjf.org/en/insights/our-research/2026/03/millions-could-lose-health-coverage-due-to-new-rules.html" target="_blank" ><u>could lose coverage</u></a> — about half of them live in Cook County. That’s less money for hospitals that treat them.</p><p><i>Kristen Schorsch is a senior reporter at WBEZ covering public health.</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/environment-public-health/2021/10/25/inside-the-fight-to-save-chicagos-historic-mercy-hospital" >Inside the battle to save Chicago’s Historic Mercy Hospital — and what comes next</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2026/07/11/where-do-they-go-what-west-side-patients-face-after-another-hospital-closes-west-suburban-medical-center" >‘Where do they go?’ What West Side patients face after their hospital closes.</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: How we photographed Lollapalooza's energy
entries.summary: <p>This week’s top photo comes from Photojournalism Intern Jeremy Battle. Follow him on <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/big_blocboy_jb/" target="_blank" >Instagram</a>.</p><h3><b>What makes this photo important?</b></h3><p>Lollapalooza’s 35th year concluded with a day full of energetic performances and lingering mud. Documenting the fan experience and the vibe of the performance is a key part of concert photography, and Turnstile frontman Brendan Yates made it easy to do both in the same frame. Acts like Turnstile displayed a level of fan interaction you may not get from festival headliners and offered a chance to see the artist swim among a sea of impassioned music-listeners.</p><h3><b>How did you get this photo?</b></h3><p>I was fortunate to be in a photo pit with other photographers I knew, but none of us expected anyone to jump off the stage and over the barricade. The moment he did, we all ran to get the best angle we could. I wanted to position myself to see fans' expressions as Yates performed, so I chose a wider view to emphasize how many people were reaching up at him. Photographers followed as he walked across different sections of the barricade, picking out different groups of fans to sing to and energizing the crowd.</p><h3><b>Technical details:</b></h3><ul entries.title: Dear Abby: Illness, Mom's Passing and Time Have Increased Isolation
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have a chronic illness and have been on a long-term leave of absence from my job for two years now. I have always surrounded myself with good people and have been blessed with great friends and family. When I was diagnosed, everyone was supportive. There were many platitudes, not the least of which was the ole standby, "Let me know if you need anything." I have never asked anyone for anything, soldiering on and refusing to be a burden.</p><p>My mom recently passed, and I'm struggling. Now, for the first time, I need actual face time. I'm extremely lonely, and all I would like is an occasional lunch or a quick diet soda with a friend. But, Abby, no one calls or responds to any of my messages. I didn't know there was a time limit on "let me know if you need anything." I know others out there understand what I'm going through, and I wonder if you have any words of encouragement. — <i>NOT ALWAYS SUNNY IN UTAH</i></p><p><b>DEAR NOT ALWAYS SUNNY:</b> Please accept my sympathy for the loss of your mother. It's shameful that your old friends and co-workers have conveniently forgotten that they offered to help you after your diagnosis. However, because they apparently have, you will have to do something about your feelings of isolation and loneliness on your own.</p><p>My first thought is to reach out to a support group (in person or online) for the illness you have. The second would be to contact your religious adviser if you have one. Another (depending on your mobility) would be to volunteer some of your free time to a cause you believe in or become a foster for shelter animals.</p><p>Finally, rather than waiting for your phone to ring, consider going out and having an occasional lunch or soft drink so you are exposed to other people rather than sitting alone at home and becoming increasingly depressed.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My son and daughter-in-law think it's OK to have cameras on me and my husband when we watch their children. It has been going on for six years, and I'm uncomfortable babysitting them while being recorded.</p><p>I know my son and his wife watch the footage, because comments have been made about what we have discussed while babysitting. I'm tired of sucking it up and allowing this. This would mean that I probably wouldn't get to see my grandchildren anymore. What should I do? — <i>HATE BEING FILMED IN THE MIDWEST</i></p><p><b>DEAR HATE BEING FILMED:</b> Are the cameras running all the time, or just when you are babysitting? If they are on all the time, then you are not being singled out. Because you find the idea of your son and daughter-in-law listening in on what you thought were private conversations, perhaps you should start doing the babysitting at your home instead of theirs. However, if that isn't viable, you may either have to bite the bullet and accept the status quo or remove babysitting from the equation.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p>

entries.title: Without housing on South, West sides, Chicago's Black communities won't grow
entries.summary: <p>“If you don’t build it, they can’t come.”</p><p>That’s not a misquotation of the mysterious voice that spoke to Kevin Costner in the 1989 hit film, “Field of Dreams.” In that sports fantasy blockbuster, Costner’s character builds a baseball diamond in the middle of his Iowa farm in response to hearing: “If you build it, he will come.”</p><p>His field of dreams brought the ghosts of baseball legends, including Chicago White Sox great “Shoeless” Joe Jackson, to play the game they loved. It even brought the ghost of the father of Costner’s character to play a game of catch with his son in the film’s climactic scene.</p><p>No, the quote above isn’t from that iconic movie, it’s what I imagine might roll through the minds of those who finance and build housing in Chicago.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c10000" name="module-c10000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>If you don’t build homes and apartments on Chicago’s South and West sides, the Black communities there can’t grow. The same goes if you don’t provide loans to buy or renovate property or refinance home loans there. And if you don’t build affordable housing in other parts of Chicago, you won’t attract Black residents.</p><p>I’m being facetious, but take a quick look around. Where do you find affordable housing? And where is there great resistance to it? Where is the city growing? And where is Chicago losing population? The answers should give us pause.</p><p>In our real-life drama, there are no ghosts emerging from the cornfields. Instead, Black Chicagoans continue to disappear, venturing elsewhere for what they can no longer find at home. According to the 2024 American Community Survey, Chicago’s estimated Black population was just over 702,000 — that’s 114,000 less than the 2020 census count and about 480,000 less than the count in 1980.</p><p>Many have posited ideas for why Chicago has witnessed such a rapid decline of Black residents. Violence, poor schools, a sluggish job market and inequality are among the ones often cited. Another reason some Black neighborhoods may be thinning is because there just aren’t as many places to live.</p><p>Among Chicago’s community areas, the South Side’s Englewood, Douglas and West Englewood lost the most housing units between 2000 and 2020, according to my analysis of census data. Collectively, those communities lost more than 6,700 housing units during that span. Englewood and West Englewood have witnessed the sharpest declines in population since 2000 — down 42% and 38%, respectively — according to data from the Chicago Metropolitan Agency for Planning. The Douglas population has decreased by more than 20%.</p><p>Meanwhile, the four communities that make the city’s Downtown and the areas immediately surrounding it have thrived. The Loop, the Near North Side, the Near West Side and the Near South Side have witnessed the highest growth in housing units and population since 2000, the data shows. Those communities saw a collective growth of more than 72,000 housing units from 2000 to 2020. And while they haven’t been known for residential development, the population has boomed in the Loop and the Near South Side. The Loop’s population has more than doubled since 2000, and the South Loop’s has more than tripled in that time. The population in both the Near North Side and the Near West Side has grown by more than 46% since 2000.</p><p>They have embodied the notion that building breeds growth. But on the South Side, disinvestment just breeds more disinvestment.</p><p>As Black communities lose their people, they’re struggling to hold on to other precious resources. Grocery stores, pharmacies and other vital institutions are boarding up or packing up and leaving just as fast as Black residents. For sure, there are positive signs of development here and there, but not enough to erase what appears to be a slide of net loss without an end in sight.</p><p>Back in February, after seeing that 2024 Black population estimate, I wrote about all of the available land and property in Black Chicago. It’s relatively cheap compared to what you’ll find in other parts of the city. Restoring the diminishing housing stock in Black neighborhoods seems to be the clearest path to reverse things. All we need is the will, I wrote.</p><p>But, for decades, the interest and the will simply hasn’t been there. And maybe that’s not a coincidence.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/author/alden-loury" target="_blank" ><i>Alden Loury</i></a><i> is data projects editor for WBEZ and writes a column for the Sun-Times.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-440000" name="module-440000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Chicago parents expect to outspend U.S. average on back-to-school supplies, survey shows
entries.summary: <p>Mollie Vivoda was squinting at her cellphone while also holding shopping lists at a Target in Bucktown on Wednesday.</p><p>Her three children will be starting school in a couple weeks, and her two daughters joined her for the family's first back-to-school shopping trip. The girls, set to start third and sixth grade, were abuzz with excitement. Vivoda's 11-year-old daughter, twin brother and 8-year-old daughter all attend a Chicago Public School in North Center.</p><p>“It’s kind of early for us [to be shopping],” Vivoda, 41, said. “This is just like our launching point. Once [I] tick off everything we got here, then I’ll probably do more comparison shopping.”</p><p>As CPS students return to class Aug. 24, parents are juggling lengthy school supply lists — at a time when inflation is making everything pricier. </p><p>Chicago K-12 parents, surveyed by Deloitte, expect to spend a whopping $794 per child on back-to-school items this year, up 7% year over year. It's also 35% higher than the national average spend $557 per child. The survey reported children's preferences influenced their parents to spend more and splurge on items.</p><p>But Matt Adams, principal at Deloitte, said 39% were "hyper-value seekers," meaning they'll shop strategically to save, like buying in bulk or using private labels.</p><p>"While consumers are planning on spending more this back-to-school season, they are also still very much seeking to stretch their dollar as far as it will go," Adams said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" A fuzzy pink cherry pom pom charm dangled off the attached lunchbox and the backpack set included matching stationery, a multicolored flower pen and binder clips.</p><p>Among the rows of standard folders, binders and notebooks were colorful displays meant to be a young girl’s dream. One large display consisted entirely of ways to decorate a reusable water bottle, with beaded charms, stickers and stick-on hooks. One sticker, like a heart-shaped waffle with the phrase, “I love you a waffle lot,” cost $3.99.</p><p>“Back-to-school shopping is a breath of fresh air,” 11-year-old Dottie Vivoda whispered, as she dumped supplies into the shopping cart.</p><p>But for some parents, this school year may be less joyful and more of a financial pain.</p><p>“We saw this huge shift towards shopping early last year, and now, it's totally dispersed,” JLL Manager of Retail Research Keisha Virtue said. The previous record was $41.5 billion in 2023.</p><p>The NRF found consumers aren't willing to compromise on fulfilling their kids needs, with 37% of respondents saying they'd rather cut back on other areas to save. And 20% said they would use buy now, pay later services like Afterpay or Klarna.</p><p>The highest spending categories are often clothing and shoes, as well as technology products, experts said. Data from the NRF said shoppers will spend an average of $250.29 on clothing and accessories, $293.11 on electronics and $174.01 on shoes.</p><p>Illinois residents will receive some relief on their back-to-school spending, due to provisions in the state’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/06/16/pritzker-signs-illinois-budget-trump-social-media-tax" >2026-27 fiscal year budget</a>. data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A shopper checks out the back-to-school section at a Target in Bucktown. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jeremy Battle/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Karen Mannerino, a mom to three CPS students, aged seven to 16, used to spend less on school supplies. Her two youngest attend Wildwood Elementary and like many Chicago schools, parents can buy a prepackaged box with required school supplies.</p><p>She said this year’s box costs $125 per child. Mannerino decided to shop around for cheaper items at Target and Amazon.</p><p>“I feel like we used to be able to buy supplies for under $100, and now, it is like it just keeps going up more and more over $100,” she said. “We used to [shop] in person. Then some years, we bought the box. This year, I just felt like the box price was so much that I could probably get it cheaper if I bought it on my own.”</p><p>Belmont Cragin resident Suggey Cortez noticed prices increasing for items like headphones and backpacks. Two of her kids attend John Barry Elementary School, and her third child, an 8th grade at charter school Intrinsic, needs more costly items, like an advanced calculator.</p><p>Cortez usually spends about $200 on required school supplies for her three kids. She estimates that may increase this year to $300, or even $400. </p><p>Groundwork Collaborative and The Century Foundation in a report last month found the price of typical school supplies increased 7.7% over the past year. It noted sharp price increases from 2025 for items like lunch boxes, which jumped by 26.8%, notebooks, up 23%, and index cards, which rose 22.2%.</p><p>The analysis pointed toward tariffs as a factor for the higher prices. It said companies such as Newell Brands, owner of Paper Mate and Elmer's glue, Logitech and ACCO Brands, parent company of Five Star and Mead notebooks, increased their prices recently because of tariffs and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/economy/2026/06/11/spiking-gas-prices-chicagoans-stop-rising-food-prices-inflation" >rising oil prices</a> as a result of the U.S.-Israel war against Iran. </p><p>While school supply lists don’t appear to have more items than usual, the lists for Mannerino and Vivoda’s children still had more than 20 items. And many schools require parents to purchase certain items in bulk for the classroom or school, such as tissues, hand sanitizer and cleaning wipes.</p><p>Vivoda typically spends at least $300 on school supplies for her three children, with about half that total toward cleaning supplies requested by the school.</p><p>But for many Chicago K-12 parents, the most expensive part of back-to-school shopping are the fees. </p><p>Before the school year begins, Mannerino will have to pay more than $885 in fees for her three children. Most of that — $585 — is for<b> </b>Lane Tech College Prep High School, where her 16-year-old is a junior. There are class-specific fees, like for art and language, and fees for technology, she said. She pays between $150 to $170 annually for each of her other two children.</p><p>Cortez said she'll be paying $150 to her son's charter school, while her second and fourth grader's supply list each includes a $30 "school fee."</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-fa0000" name="module-fa0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h4>5 Ways to Slash Back-to-School Spending</h4><br>It can be hard to manage back-to-school spending in an environment where prices are higher on many everyday items, including gas and groceries.<br><br>Here’s five ways to cut costs without sacrificing quality.<br><br><b>Shorten your shopping list</b><br><br>Try shopping your home first, California-based money-saving expert Andrea Woroch said.<br><br>“Look to see what you already have. You can reuse pencil cases and binders,” she said. Sometimes, a composition notebook from a previous year has only a few pages used, so you can simply remove those pages and reuse the notebook.<br><br>You don’t need to buy the pricier items new every year either, said Kristian Brennon, a Kansas-based accredited financial counselor. If you know families with older children, you might be able to score gently used hand-me-downs and skip the stores altogether.<br><br><b>Check on community resources</b><br><br>Many communities have consignment sales, back-to-school fairs and freecycling events in advance of the new school year to help you save on supplies and clothes. Community members can trade items and pick up what they need for a low price or free, Brennon said.<br><br>Sell or consign some of the stuff your kids have outgrown to generate some extra cash for this year’s back-to-school expenses, she adds.<br><br>Band together with other caregivers in your grade to buy items — like notebooks and folders — in bulk at a lower price.<br><br><b>Seek out the deals</b><br><br>Big-box stores like Walmart and Target are offering back-to-school sales comparable to the ones they’ve run in years past.<br><br>Store-brand notebooks tend to be much cheaper than name-brand ones, Woroch says, even though the product is virtually identical. Plus, she says, some brands — like Hanna Andersson and Athleta Girl — offer pre-loved sections online, which makes it easier to snag lower prices on gently-used clothing.<br><br><b>Plan ahead with a sinking fund</b><br><br>A sinking fund is a savings account dedicated to a specific expense, like back-to-school. You deposit money into it regularly throughout the year so you can use it instead of your paycheck when it’s time to buy.<br><br>Otherwise, it’s easy to forget the cost is coming up.<br><br><b>Give your kids a budget</b><br><br>For some parents, figuring out how to budget for back-to-school shopping begins with a conversation with their kids about money.<br><br>“Create a list together and set expectations,” New York-based shopping expert Trae Bodge said. “We might not be able to get everything our kids want.”<br><br>That discussion can help kids build financial literacy. For preteens and teens, if they want a brand-name item, perhaps they can contribute to the cost through extra chores, their allowance or a summer job, Bodge said.<br><br><i>— Kimberly Palmer, NerdWallet</i></div> </div><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board/2026/07/30/chicago-school-board-approves-budget-that-reverses-layoffs-but-counts-on-shaky-state-funds" >Chicago School Board approves budget that reverses layoffs, but counts on shaky state funds</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
